```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# This chunk creates the SVG diagrams used later in the slides. It does not print in the HTML.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
# Change these values to change the colours throughout the diagrams.
reading_blue <- "#003b70"
reading_teal <- "#008c95"
reading_pink <- "#e5007d"
reading_orange <- "#e84e0f"
grid_col <- "#d9e1e5"

# Common axes and grid styling for all plots below; plot() supplies the axis labels.
plot_theme <- function() {
  axis(1, col = "#555555", col.axis = "#252525", lwd = 1.2)
  axis(2, col = "#555555", col.axis = "#252525", lwd = 1.2, las = 1)
  box(bty = "l", col = "#555555", lwd = 1.2)
  grid(col = grid_col, lty = 1)
}

# PPF: stage 0 = curve; 1 = A; 2 = move to B; 3 = trade-off annotations.
ppf_frame <- function(file, stage) {
  svg(file, width = 9, height = 4.8, bg = "white")
  par(mar = c(4.2, 4.5, 0.5, 1.0))
  x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)
  y <- 10 - 0.10 * x^2  # Edit this expression to change the frontier's shape.
  plot(x, y, type = "n", xlim = c(0, 10.5), ylim = c(0, 10.5),
       xlab = "Capital goods", ylab = "Consumption goods", axes = FALSE)
  plot_theme()
  lines(x, y, lwd = 3, col = reading_blue)
  text(7.8, 4.8, "PPF", col = reading_blue, font = 2)
  if (stage >= 1) {
    # Point and label coordinates are fixed: update them if the PPF changes.
    points(3, 9.1, pch = 19, cex = 1.7, col = reading_pink)
    text(3.25, 9.65, "A", col = reading_pink, font = 2)
  }
  if (stage >= 2) {
    arrows(3.35, 8.85, 6.55, 5.25, length = .12, lwd = 2.5, col = reading_orange)
    points(7, 5.1, pch = 19, cex = 1.7, col = reading_orange)
    text(7.25, 5.6, "B", col = reading_orange, font = 2)
  }
  if (stage >= 3) {
    segments(3, 0, 3, 9.1, lty = 2, col = "#777777")
    segments(7, 0, 7, 5.1, lty = 2, col = "#777777")
    text(5.15, 1.1, "more investment today", col = reading_orange, font = 2)
    text(5.15, 9.5, "less consumption today", col = reading_pink, font = 2)
  }
  dev.off()
}

# Combined market: stage 0 = curves; 1 = equilibrium; 2 = price/quantity guides.
# shock selects an extra demand or supply curve for the later shock slides.
market_frame <- function(file, stage, shock = "none") {
  svg(file, width = 9, height = 4.8, bg = "white")
  par(mar = c(4.2, 4.5, 0.5, 1.0))
  q <- seq(0, 55, length.out = 200)
  demand <- 50 - 0.5 * q  # Inverse demand: price as a function of quantity.
  supply <- 10 + 0.5 * q  # Inverse supply. These meet at Q = 40, P = 30.
  plot(q, demand, type = "n", xlim = c(0, 58), ylim = c(0, 55),
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "Quantity", ylab = "Price")
  plot_theme()
  lines(q, demand, lwd = 3, col = reading_blue)
  lines(q, supply, lwd = 3, col = reading_teal)
  text(50, 23, "D", col = reading_blue, font = 2)
  text(50, 37, "S", col = reading_teal, font = 2)
  # Equilibrium points, guides, and shift endpoints below use fixed coordinates.
  # If you edit a curve equation, recalculate these coordinates too.
  if (stage >= 1) {
    points(40, 30, pch = 19, cex = 1.6, col = reading_pink)
    text(42, 31.8, "E", col = reading_pink, font = 2)
  }
  if (stage >= 2) {
    segments(0, 30, 40, 30, lty = 2, col = "#777777")
    segments(40, 0, 40, 30, lty = 2, col = "#777777")
    text(2.5, 31.8, expression(P^"*"), col = reading_pink, font = 2)
    text(40, 2.5, expression(Q^"*"), col = reading_pink, font = 2)
  }
  if (shock == "demand") {
    demand2 <- 57.5 - 0.5 * q
    lines(q, demand2, lwd = 3, col = reading_orange)
    text(53, 32, expression(D[1]), col = reading_orange, font = 2)
    arrows(25, 39, 32, 42.5, length = .12, lwd = 2.3, col = reading_orange)
    points(47.5, 33.75, pch = 19, cex = 1.6, col = reading_orange)
    segments(0, 33.75, 47.5, 33.75, lty = 2, col = reading_orange)
    segments(47.5, 0, 47.5, 33.75, lty = 2, col = reading_orange)
  }
  if (shock == "supply") {
    supply2 <- 17.5 + 0.5 * q
    lines(q, supply2, lwd = 3, col = reading_orange)
    text(50, 44, expression(S[1]), col = reading_orange, font = 2)
    arrows(32, 26, 25, 30, length = .12, lwd = 2.3, col = reading_orange)
    points(32.5, 33.75, pch = 19, cex = 1.6, col = reading_orange)
    segments(0, 33.75, 32.5, 33.75, lty = 2, col = reading_orange)
    segments(32.5, 0, 32.5, 33.75, lty = 2, col = reading_orange)
  }
  dev.off()
}

# Generate every stage once. Later slides display these files using <img> tags.
invisible(lapply(0:3, function(i) ppf_frame(sprintf("figures/ppf-%s.svg", i), i)))
invisible(lapply(0:2, function(i) market_frame(sprintf("figures/equilibrium-%s.svg", i), i)))
market_frame("figures/demand-shift.svg", 2, "demand")
market_frame("figures/supply-shift.svg", 2, "supply")

# A curve on its own: kind chooses demand/supply; stage 0 = curve,
# 1 = movement along it, and 2 = a new shifted curve.
single_curve_frame <- function(file, kind, stage) {
  svg(file, width = 8.5, height = 4.3, bg = "white")
  par(mar = c(4.1, 4.5, 0.4, 0.8))
  q <- seq(0, 55, length.out = 200)
  demand_curve <- kind == "demand"
  price <- if (demand_curve) 50 - 0.5 * q else 10 + 0.5 * q
  plot(q, price, type = "n", xlim = c(0, 58), ylim = c(0, 55),
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "Quantity", ylab = "Price")
  plot_theme()
  curve_col <- if (demand_curve) reading_blue else reading_teal
  lines(q, price, lwd = 3, col = curve_col)
  text(51, if (demand_curve) 22 else 37,
       if (demand_curve) "D" else "S", col = curve_col, font = 2)
  # A and B mark a price change on the same curve. Move their coordinates
  # if you change the curve equations above.
  if (stage >= 1) {
    p1 <- if (demand_curve) 38 else 22
    p2 <- if (demand_curve) 30 else 30
    q1 <- if (demand_curve) 24 else 24
    q2 <- if (demand_curve) 40 else 40
    points(c(q1, q2), c(p1, p2), pch = 19, cex = 1.4, col = reading_pink)
    text(q1 - 2.4, p1 + 2.7, "A", col = reading_pink, font = 2)
    text(q2 + 2.3, p2 + 2.5, "B", col = reading_pink, font = 2)
    arrows(q1 + 2, p1 - 1, q2 - 2, p2 + 1,
           length = .12, lwd = 2.2, col = reading_pink)
  }
  if (stage >= 2) {
    shifted <- if (demand_curve) 57.5 - 0.5 * q else 17.5 + 0.5 * q
    lines(q, shifted, lwd = 3, col = reading_orange)
    text(51, if (demand_curve) 30 else 44,
         if (demand_curve) expression(D[1]) else expression(S[1]),
         col = reading_orange, font = 2)
    arrows(25, if (demand_curve) 39 else 22,
           if (demand_curve) 32 else 18,
           if (demand_curve) 42.5 else 29.5,
           length = .12, lwd = 2.2, col = reading_orange)
  }
  dev.off()
}
invisible(lapply(0:2, function(i) single_curve_frame(sprintf("figures/demand-%s.svg", i), "demand", i)))
invisible(lapply(0:2, function(i) single_curve_frame(sprintf("figures/supply-%s.svg", i), "supply", i)))
```

## Micro foundations for macroeconomics

**Macro I**

This short review revisits the microeconomic ideas we will use to understand economy-wide outcomes.

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

- use a production possibility frontier to explain scarcity, opportunity cost, and comparative advantage;
- distinguish movements along demand and supply curves from shifts in those curves;
- solve a market equilibrium and predict the effect of a demand or supply shock;
- explain where this microeconomic toolkit appears in macroeconomics.

### 📚 Reading

Case, Fair, and Oster, *Principles of Macroeconomics*, Chapters 2, 3, and 4.

## Why micro matters for macro

Macroeconomics studies totals, but those totals come from connected decisions.

| Micro foundation | Later use in Macro I |
|---|---|
| scarcity and opportunity cost | consumption, saving, and public spending choices |
| production possibilities | productive capacity and long-run growth |
| demand and supply | goods, labour, and financial markets |
| equilibrium and comparative statics | output, employment, interest rates, and prices |
| elasticity and surplus | responsiveness and the gains from exchange |

The same method recurs: 

- specify behaviour
- impose constraints 
- solve equilibrium
- change one assumption

## Scarcity creates an economic problem

Scarcity means that available resources cannot satisfy every possible use.

It forces three linked questions:

- What should the economy produce?
- How should it combine labour, capital, and natural resources?
- Who receives the resulting goods and services?

The constraint may involve time, productive capacity, finance, or institutions.

## Opportunity cost identifies the relevant trade-off

The **opportunity cost** of an action is the value of the best alternative forgone.

Suppose your next two hours could be used for:

| Choice | Value to you |
|---|---:|
| attend the lecture | £32 |
| work a paid shift | £24 |
| revise independently | £18 |
| meet friends | £15 |

If you attend, the opportunity cost is **£24**, not £57 and not zero.

## A production possibility frontier

A **production possibility frontier (PPF)** shows the maximum feasible combinations of two outputs, given resources and technology.

- Points **on** the frontier use resources efficiently.
- Points **inside** the frontier are feasible but inefficient.
- Points **outside** the frontier are not currently feasible.

The frontier describes a constraint. Preferences determine which feasible point society chooses.

An interior point may reflect unused labour or other resources. 

More resources or better technology can shift the frontier outwards.

## Current consumption and future capacity

<div class="plot-stack"><img src="figures/ppf-0.svg" alt="Production possibility frontier"><ul class="incremental plot-overlays"><li><img src="figures/ppf-1.svg" alt="Point A on the production possibility frontier"></li><li><img src="figures/ppf-2.svg" alt="Movement from point A to point B"></li><li><img src="figures/ppf-3.svg" alt="Trade-off between current consumption and capital goods"></li></ul></div>

<div class="plot-caption">The production possibility frontier (PPF) shows the trade-off between capital goods and consumption goods. Advance to reveal A, the move to B, and the opportunity cost.</div>

## Reading the slope of the PPF

The slope of the **production possibility frontier (PPF)** measures opportunity cost: how many consumption goods must be given up for one more capital good.

<div class="equation-box">
$$\text{Opportunity cost of one more capital good}
= -\frac{\Delta \text{consumption goods}}{\Delta \text{capital goods}}$$
</div>

Moving towards more capital goods sacrifices current consumption. Economists call the absolute value of this slope the **marginal rate of transformation (MRT)**.

The frontier **curves outwards from the origin** and gets steeper as we move right. 

Each additional capital good then requires giving up more consumption goods, because resources differ in their suitability across uses.

## Comparative advantage and specialisation

Imagine Robinson Crusoe living alone on an island. Friday joins him. Both can fish or collect coconuts, but at different rates.

| In one hour | Robinson Crusoe | Friday |
|---|---:|---:|
| Fish | 12 | 6 |
| Coconuts | 6 | 12 |

One fish costs Robinson **½ coconut** but Friday **2 coconuts**. Robinson has a **comparative advantage** in fish; Friday has one in coconuts.

If each divides the hour equally, together they produce **9 fish and 9 coconuts**. If Robinson fishes and Friday collects coconuts, they produce **12 of each**. Specialisation creates scope for trade.

## Markets coordinate separate decisions

Households and firms make plans independently.

The market price carries information and provides an incentive to revise those plans.

- Demand describes buyers' planned purchases.
- Supply describes sellers' planned production.
- Equilibrium makes the plans mutually consistent.

Quantity demanded and quantity supplied are flows measured over a stated period.

## Demand as a function

For a good $x$, quantity demanded depends on its own price and other determinants:

$$Q_x^d=D(P_x,Y,W,P_r,T,E,N).$$

| Symbol | Meaning | Effect on demand for $x$ |
|---|---|---|
| $P_x$ | own price | higher $P_x$ usually lowers $Q_x^d$ |
| $Y$, $W$ | household income, wealth | usually raise demand for a normal good |
| $P_r$ | prices of related goods | depends on substitutes or complements |
| $T$, $E$, $N$ | tastes, expectations, number of buyers | depends on the change |

The **demand curve** varies $P_x$ while holding $Y,W,P_r,T,E,N$ fixed. Changes in these other determinants shift the curve.

## Movement along demand or a shift?

$$Q^d = a - bP, \qquad b>0.$$

<div class="concept-plot plot-stack"><img src="figures/demand-0.svg" alt="Downward-sloping demand curve"><ul class="incremental plot-overlays"><li><img src="figures/demand-1.svg" alt="A rise in price moves along the demand curve from B to A"></li><li><img src="figures/demand-2.svg" alt="A change in another determinant shifts demand to the right"></li></ul></div>

<div class="plot-caption">First, change the good's own price: move along D. Then, change another determinant: D shifts.</div>

Higher own price usually lowers quantity demanded through substitution and income effects. 

The inverse form, $P=(a-Q^d)/b$, puts price on the vertical axis.

## Train journeys and the bus fare

Suppose weekly demand is:

$$Q^d = 80 - 4P + 0.02Y + 2P_b,$$

where $P$ is the rail fare, $Y$ is weekly income, and $P_b$ is the bus fare.

At $P=20$, $Y=1{,}000$, and $P_b=10$:

$$Q^d = 80 - 80 + 20 + 20 = 40.$$

If the bus fare rises to 15, demand for train journeys rises to 50. The positive cross-price effect identifies the two services as substitutes.

## Household demand and total spending

Suppose many households expect higher incomes next year and bring forward some purchases.

<ul class="incremental">
<li><strong>One market:</strong> demand for goods such as furniture rises. At the original price, planned purchases exceed available supply.</li>
<li><strong>Across the economy:</strong> income, wealth, and expectations influence how much households plan to spend. Changes shared by many households affect planned aggregate expenditure.</li>
<li><strong>Important distinction:</strong> a market demand curve varies the price of one good. Macroeconomic demand concerns total spending and the overall price level; it is not obtained by simply adding these single-good diagrams.</li>
</ul>

## Supply as a function

For a good $x$, quantity supplied depends on its own price and production conditions:

$$Q_x^s=S(P_x,P_i,A,P_o,N_f,E).$$

| Symbol | Meaning | Effect on supply of $x$ |
|---|---|---|
| $P_x$ | own price | higher $P_x$ usually raises $Q_x^s$ |
| $P_i$ | input prices | higher costs usually reduce supply |
| $A$ | productivity or technology | improvements usually raise supply |
| $P_o$ | prices of other goods firms could produce | firms may switch production |
| $N_f$, $E$ | number of firms, expected future prices | depends on the change and timing |

The **supply curve** varies $P_x$ while holding other determinants fixed. Changes in them shift the curve.

## Movement along supply or a shift?

$$Q^s = c + dP, \qquad d>0.$$

<div class="concept-plot plot-stack"><img src="figures/supply-0.svg" alt="Upward-sloping supply curve"><ul class="incremental plot-overlays"><li><img src="figures/supply-1.svg" alt="A rise in price moves along the supply curve from A to B"></li><li><img src="figures/supply-2.svg" alt="Higher input costs shift supply to the left"></li></ul></div>

<div class="plot-caption">First, change the good's own price: move along S. Then, raise input costs: S shifts left.</div>

Increasing marginal cost helps explain the upward slope. 

The inverse form, $P=(Q^s-c)/d$, puts price on the vertical axis.

## Bakery output and input costs

Suppose daily supply is:

$$Q^s = -20 + 3P - 0.5W + 4A,$$

where $P$ is the bakery's output price, $W$ is an input-cost index, and $A$ is a productivity index.

At $P=20$, $W=40$, and $A=5$:

$$Q^s = -20 + 60 - 20 + 20 = 40.$$

If $W$ rises to 52, supply falls to 34 at the same price. That is a leftward shift, not movement along the supply curve.

## Firm supply and total output

Suppose energy becomes more expensive for many producers, not only the bakery.

<ul class="incremental">
<li><strong>One market:</strong> higher input costs reduce the quantity a firm is willing to supply at each output price. Its supply curve shifts left.</li>
<li><strong>Across the economy:</strong> wages, energy prices, and productivity influence costs in many industries at once. These common conditions matter for total production.</li>
<li><strong>Longer-run contrast:</strong> a broad improvement in productivity lets firms produce more with given resources. This links firm supply to the outward shift of the production possibility frontier.</li>
</ul>

## Market equilibrium

Equilibrium requires planned purchases to equal planned sales:

$$Q^d(P^*) = Q^s(P^*).$$

The equilibrium price $P^*$ is **endogenous** because the model determines it.

Income, technology, and input costs are **exogenous** in this simple model because we take them as given. A larger macro model may determine them too.

Here we clear **one product market**. Macroeconomic equilibrium must also account for interactions with the labour and financial markets.

## Solving equilibrium with equations

Suppose:

$$Q^d = 100 - 2P, \qquad Q^s = 10 + P.$$

Set demand equal to supply:

$$100 - 2P = 10 + P.$$

Therefore:

$$P^* = 30, \qquad Q^* = 40.$$

Always substitute the price back into both equations. Each must return the same quantity.

## Equilibrium on the graph

<div class="plot-stack"><img src="figures/equilibrium-0.svg" alt="Demand and supply curves"><ul class="incremental plot-overlays"><li><img src="figures/equilibrium-1.svg" alt="Equilibrium point"></li><li><img src="figures/equilibrium-2.svg" alt="Equilibrium price and quantity"></li></ul></div>

<div class="plot-caption">Advance to reveal the equilibrium point, then its price and quantity.</div>

## Disequilibrium creates pressure for adjustment

At a price below equilibrium:

$$Q^d > Q^s.$$

There is excess demand. Buyers compete for scarce output and the price tends to rise.

At a price above equilibrium:

$$Q^s > Q^d.$$

There is excess supply. Unsold inventories encourage sellers to reduce the price or production.

The speed and form of adjustment depend on institutions. Prices do not always change instantly.

## Comparative statics

Comparative statics compares one equilibrium with another after an exogenous change.

1. Identify the variable that changed.
2. Decide which curve shifts and in which direction.
3. Find the new intersection.
4. State the changes in equilibrium price and quantity.

The method compares endpoints. It does not describe the time path between them.

## An increase in demand

<div class="plot-stack shock-plot"><img src="figures/equilibrium-2.svg" alt="Initial market equilibrium"><ul class="incremental plot-overlays"><li><img src="figures/demand-shift.svg" alt="Demand shifts right and equilibrium price and quantity rise"></li></ul></div>

**Macro connection:** 

<ul class="incremental shock-notes">
<li>If many households bring purchases forward, planned aggregate expenditure rises.</li>
<li>With spare capacity, firms can increase <strong>output and employment</strong>.</li>
<li>When capacity is tight, more of the response may appear in the <strong>overall price level</strong>.</li>
<li>The single-market diagram shows the direction of a shift, but it does not determine the economy-wide split between output and prices.</li>
</ul>

## An adverse supply shock

<div class="plot-stack shock-plot"><img src="figures/equilibrium-2.svg" alt="Initial market equilibrium"><ul class="incremental plot-overlays"><li><img src="figures/supply-shift.svg" alt="Supply shifts left, price rises and quantity falls"></li></ul></div>

**Macro connection:** 

<ul class="incremental shock-notes">
<li>If energy costs rise across many industries, producing the same total output becomes more expensive.</li>
<li><strong>Real output may fall</strong> while the <strong>overall price level may rise</strong>.</li>
<li>Firms' responses also depend on wages, productivity, and demand, so a single-market graph cannot by itself quantify the economy-wide effect.</li>
</ul>

## Two shifts may leave one outcome ambiguous

Suppose demand rises while supply falls.

- Both shifts raise the equilibrium price.
- The demand shift raises equilibrium quantity.
- The supply shift lowers equilibrium quantity.

Price therefore rises, but the change in quantity depends on the relative sizes of the shifts.

This is a general identification lesson: observing price alone rarely tells us which shock occurred.

## Elasticity measures responsiveness

Price elasticity of demand:

$$\varepsilon_d = \frac{\%\Delta Q^d}{\%\Delta P}.$$

Price elasticity of supply:

$$\varepsilon_s = \frac{\%\Delta Q^s}{\%\Delta P}.$$

Use percentage changes because slopes depend on units. Demand is elastic when \(|\varepsilon_d|>1\) and inelastic when \(|\varepsilon_d|<1\).

Elasticities help predict the size of price and quantity adjustments after a shock.


## Worked diagnostic

For each event, identify the curve, direction, and predicted equilibrium changes.

| Event | First-round market effect |
|---|---|
| household income rises for a normal good | demand shifts right; price rises, quantity rises |
| energy costs rise | supply shifts left; price rises, quantity falls |
| productivity improves | supply shifts right; price falls, quantity rises |
| expected future price rises | current demand may rise; current supply may fall |

The final row needs a model of timing. Expectations can affect both sides of a market.

## Summary

- Scarcity makes opportunity cost unavoidable.
- The PPF separates feasibility, efficiency, utilisation, and growth.
- Demand and supply functions distinguish movements along curves from shifts.
- Equilibrium makes independent plans consistent; comparative statics traces the effect of shocks.
- Elasticity helps predict the size of adjustment.
- The same logic underpins macro models, but aggregation introduces new mechanisms.
